opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. Honestly, I'd say the bottleneck has shifted over time. Early on, when I was working on physics simulation and graphics, the limit was very concrete: I didn't know enough math, I didn't know enough about compilers, and I didn't have the engineering skills to build the systems I imagined. So I just spent years filling those gaps. Building Taichi was in many ways a result of that, because I kept hitting the same wall of writing high-performance simulation code by hand, and eventually I thought, why not build a language that solves this once and for all?

These days I feel the limitation is less about technical skill and more about judgment. Technical problems usually yield if you put enough hours into them. The harder questions are which problems are actually worth solving, how to get a team aligned, how to make something people will really use, and how to balance ambition with what's realistic in a given time frame. Those don't have clean answers, and I'm still learning them, often by making mistakes.

There's also a scale issue. As an individual researcher, my ability to solve problems was roughly the ceiling of what I could do. But the things I care about now, like making 3D content creation accessible to everyone, are much bigger than any one person. So the question becomes whether I can build an organization whose problem-solving ability is much greater than my own. That's a very different skill, and I'd say it's currently the main thing between me and the ambitions I have.

So I try not to see it as a fixed ceiling. I see it as the next thing to work on. Every few years the constraint moves somewhere new, and I think that's a good sign. It means you're still growing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think about this a lot. When I started working on Taichi, the ambition was pretty simple: I wanted to make writing high-performance graphics and physics simulation code as easy as writing Python. That sounds modest, but the gap between "I can write a working simulation in a notebook" and "this runs on a GPU at interactive framerates" is enormous, and most of my career has been about shrinking that gap.

The way I see it, your ability to solve problems is really the ceiling on what you can even imagine attempting. Early on, when I was doing research at MIT, I could only solve problems that fit in one person's head. A compiler, a renderer, a fluid solver, each one was a project I could carry alone. That shaped my ambitions. I wasn't thinking about building infrastructure that thousands of people would depend on, because I had no idea how to do that.

Then you start a company, and suddenly the constraint shifts. It's no longer "can I write this algorithm," it's "can I get a team of people to build something coherent, can I understand what users actually need rather than what I find intellectually interesting, can I make tradeoffs between research purity and shipping." Those are problems too, and I was pretty bad at them at first. So for a while, my ambitions were honestly limited more by my weakness as an organizer and communicator than by anything technical.

What I've come to believe is that the limiting factor keeps moving. Right now, a lot of what we want to do in simulation and in AI for physical systems is bottlenecked less by any single clever idea and more by the ability to make the whole stack work together: data, compilers, hardware, the people who use it. If I'm being self-critical, my instinct is still to retreat into the part I know I can solve, which is the hard technical kernel, when the thing that actually limits the ambition is everything around it.

So I'd put it this way: my current problem-solving ability doesn't so much limit what I want to do as it shapes what I think is realistic. And I try to deliberately pick goals that are a bit beyond what I can currently solve, because that's the only way the ceiling moves. If I only chose problems I already knew how to crack, I'd just be repeating my PhD over and over.

astra-6.text:
I think my ambitions are always a little ahead of my ability to solve problems. I can imagine something I want to build, but I don’t necessarily know how to get there yet. That gap helps me figure out what I need to learn and where I need help.

The tricky part is choosing a problem that stretches you without being so far beyond your abilities that you can’t make progress. I try to find a smaller piece I can solve, learn from that, and then take on the next piece. So my current ability limits where I can start, but I don’t think it has to determine where I end up.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my ambitions are always a little ahead of my ability to solve problems. You can imagine something very exciting, but then you have to ask, what’s the first concrete step? Can I actually make that work? And often, that’s where you discover what you still need to learn.

But I don’t see my current ability as a fixed ceiling. I can learn, try a different approach, or work with people who have complementary skills. So it influences where I start and how quickly I can move, more than what I’m willing to aim for.
